blocks.content: Agriculture of India is not only an economic activity but also a way of life for millions of people. This chapter explains agriculture from geographical, climatic, economic and social perspectives. Every concept is expanded step-by-step so that even a beginner can understand it clearly, while the depth is sufficient for SSC, State PCS and other competitive examinations.
PART A: AGRICULTURE – BASIC CONCEPT & ROLE

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Indian agriculture relies heavily on physical factors, soil-crop relationships, and climatic requirements across regions.
Farming practices are categorized into Subsistence, Intensive, Commercial, and Plantation Agriculture.
Cropping patterns in India are divided into three distinct seasons: Kharif, Rabi, and Zaid.
Major crops encompass food grains (Rice, Wheat, Coarse Grains & Millets) and various Cash Crops.
The Green Revolution brought significant technological achievements while introducing specific regional and ecological limitations.

blocks.content: Meaning of Agriculture
Agriculture refers to the practice of cultivating crops and rearing animals for food, fibre, fuel and other products. It includes crop production, livestock, fisheries and forestry.
Role of Agriculture in Indian Economy

Agriculture employs a large portion of India’s population and supports rural livelihoods. It provides food for the population, raw materials for agro-based industries, contributes to exports and ensures food security.
Nature of Indian Agriculture

Indian agriculture is largely dependent on monsoon rainfall. It is characterised by small and fragmented landholdings, traditional farming practices, labour-intensive cultivation and wide regional diversity.
PART B: DETAILED FACTORS AFFECTING AGRICULTURE
Physical Factors

Physical factors include relief, soil, climate, temperature, rainfall and water availability. Flat plains, fertile soils and adequate rainfall support intensive agriculture, while hilly areas and arid regions restrict farming.
Soil and Crop Relationship
Different crops require different types of soil. For example, rice grows well in clayey soil, wheat in alluvial soil, cotton in black soil and tea in laterite soil.
Climatic Requirements of Crops
Temperature, rainfall and humidity decide cropping patterns. Monsoon plays a crucial role in deciding the success or failure of crops.
Human Factors
Human factors include size of landholdings, irrigation facilities, use of fertilizers, HYV seeds, mechanisation, access to credit, transport facilities and government policies.
PART C: TYPES OF FARMING (IN-DEPTH)
Subsistence Farming
Subsistence farming is practiced mainly to meet the needs of the farmer’s family. It is characterised by small landholdings, traditional tools and low productivity.
Intensive Farming
Intensive farming involves the use of large amounts of labour, capital, fertilizers and irrigation on small land areas to increase output.
Commercial Farming
Commercial farming aims at producing crops for sale in the market. It involves use of modern technology and inputs.
Plantation Agriculture
Plantation agriculture is a type of commercial farming where a single crop is grown on large estates using hired labour. Tea, coffee and rubber are important plantation crops.
PART D: CROPPING PATTERN & SEASONS (FULL DETAIL)
Kharif Crops
Kharif crops are sown at the beginning of the southwest monsoon and harvested in autumn. They require high temperature and rainfall.
Rabi Crops
Rabi crops are sown in winter and harvested in spring. They grow well in cool climate with moderate rainfall.
Zaid Crops
Zaid crops are grown during the short summer season between Rabi and Kharif. They require irrigation.
PART E: MAJOR CROPS OF INDIA (CROP-WISE DETAIL)
Rice
Rice is the most important food crop of India. It requires high temperature, heavy rainfall and clayey soil. It is mainly grown in eastern and southern India.
Wheat
Wheat is a major rabi crop. It requires cool climate during growth and warm climate during harvest.
Coarse Grains & Millets
Millets like jowar, bajra and ragi are grown in dry regions. They are hardy crops requiring less rainfall.
Cash Crops
Cash crops include sugarcane, cotton, jute, tea and coffee. These crops are important for industries and exports.
PART F: IRRIGATION SYSTEM IN INDIA
Importance of Irrigation
Irrigation reduces dependence on monsoon and increases cropping intensity.
Sources of Irrigation
Canals, wells, tube wells, tanks and modern irrigation methods like drip and sprinkler systems are used.

blocks.content: PART G: GREEN REVOLUTION (COMPLETE ANALYSIS)
Meaning and Features
Green Revolution involved the use of HYV seeds, fertilizers, irrigation and modern agricultural practices.
Achievements and Limitations
It increased food grain production but caused regional imbalance, soil degradation and environmental problems.
PART H: PROBLEMS & CHALLENGES OF INDIAN AGRICULTURE
Major Problems
Problems include small landholdings, overdependence on monsoon, low mechanisation, poor storage, marketing issues and farmer distress.
